edits.fix: Use the standard footer 'Bellingham Math Circle / Week 7 / <id>' on every page instead of a bare page number at the right margin.

edits.quote: It is your turn with a bigger pile.
edits.fix: Delete 'with a bigger pile'; the drawn piles already show this. Keep 'It is your turn.' and the instruction.

edits.quote: Show every different way a game with 4 counters can go, and then every way a game with 5 counters can go. (8 rows of 4 dots, 10 rows of 5 dots)
edits.fix: There are 5 ways for 4 counters and 8 ways for 5, so a child filling the 8 and 10 rows cannot tell when they are done. Say that taking 1 then 2 and taking 2 then 1 count as different ways. Then either print exactly 5 and 8 rows or say how many ways there are for 4 counters.

edits.quote: Diagram: in each pair box, '1st' sits directly under the left pile and '2nd' directly under the right pile
edits.fix: As placed, the choices read as labels for 'first pile' and 'second pile'. Center the 1st/2nd choice below the whole pair, clearly apart from the piles, or print 'go 1st   go 2nd'.

edits.quote: Now there is one pile again, and whoever takes the last counter loses.
edits.fix: P7 changed the moves to 1, 2, or 3, so state the moves here: 'Now there is one pile again, each player takes 1 or 2 counters, and whoever takes the last counter loses.'

k-1.summary: A real K–1 progression with correct math throughout: traps under {1,2}, testing a fixed opening move, listing every way a game can go, the {1,2,3} rule, two piles with copying, and the version where taking the last counter loses. All the diagrams have the right counts. The edits are small: one bit of narration, an unclear stopping point in P6, the 1st/2nd labels in P8 that look like pile labels, and a missing rule restatement in P10.

edits.fix: Use the standard footer 'Bellingham Math Circle / Week 7 / <id>' on every page.

edits.quote: In every game in this packet, two players take turns taking counters from a pile. Each problem says how many counters a player may take on a turn.
edits.fix: Cut the meta wording: 'Two players take turns taking counters from a pile. Whoever takes the last counter wins.'

edits.quote: Diagram: 'First' printed under the left pile and 'Second' under the right pile in each pair box
edits.fix: As placed, the choices read as names for the two piles. Center the First/Second choice below the pair, separated from the piles, or print 'go first / go second'.

edits.quote: Find a rule for how many counters a player may take on a turn, so that you would rather go second exactly when the starting pile is 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, and so on.
edits.fix: A rule without 1 (for example 2 or 3) leaves a player who cannot move, and the page does not say who wins then. Add 'A player who cannot move loses' or require that the rule allows taking 1.

grades-2-3.summary: A strong, correctly worked sequence. It moves from {1,2} to checking claimed strategies against every reply, classifying {1,3,4} up to 20 and extending it to 100 (all answers correct), a parity argument for {1,3,5}, two piles including the surprising (4,1), and inventing a rule whose losing piles are the multiples of 5, which is solvable with {1,2,3,4} and {1,2,3,4,6}. The edits are a meta sentence in the rules, a 'First/Second' label placement that reads as pile names, and an edge case in P8 where a player cannot move.

edits.fix: Use the standard footer 'Bellingham Math Circle / Week 7 / <id>' on every page.

edits.quote: In every game in this packet, two players take turns taking counters from a pile. Each problem says how many counters a player may take on a turn.
edits.fix: Cut the meta wording. Keep 'Two players take turns taking counters from a pile. Unless a problem says otherwise, whoever takes the last counter wins.'

edits.quote: Explain why the pattern of losing piles you found in Problem 1 must keep going forever, for piles of every size.
edits.fix: P2 already makes children assume the period-7 pattern for 100, 1000 and 2026, two problems before this asks why it holds. Move P5 directly after P2 so the extrapolation and its justification sit together.

edits.quote: When the two piles are the same size, which player can always win? Explain why.
edits.fix: This points only at the diagonal, which the copying argument settles at once and which the 2–3 band also does. The grid shows much more: the losing squares are exactly the pairs with the same remainder mod 3, such as (1,4), (0,3) and (2,5). Replace with 'Describe the pattern of shaded squares and explain why it works.'

edits.quote: row 0 or column 0 stands for an empty pile
edits.fix: The square at row 0, column 0 is a 'game' with no counters, and children will ask whether to shade it. Add 'With no counters left, the player to move has lost.'

grades-4-5.summary: The richest band, and every answer checks: {1,3,4} has period 7 (100 losing, 1000 take 4, 2026 take 1 or 3), the four contrasting games including {1,2,4}, which has the same pattern as {1,2}, the greedy plan failing everywhere except {1,3,5}, the four move sets with losing piles at multiples of 4, the shifted pattern when taking the last counter loses, and two-pile grids whose P9 answer is (1,3), (1,8), (3,8), (2,7), (4,6). The edits are to move the 'why it repeats' problem next to the extrapolation and to widen P8's follow-up from the diagonal to the whole pattern. There is more than a quick child can finish, but none of it is padding.

overall.strongest: The mathematics is correct and well sequenced in every band, with purposeful contrasting rules, claims tested against every reply, and two-pile games that build toward the outline's deeper ideas.
overall.weakest: Small presentation problems repeat across bands: meta wording in the rules, a nonstandard footer, First/Second labels that look like pile names, and a few follow-up questions or rule restatements that are too narrow or missing.
